report.summary: Parsed chunk 2 of parse.py: tree-sitter unit extraction, C/C++ declarator name resolution, and import record function header.
risks: line 121-148 | medium | Iterative pre-order walk uses reversed children to preserve source order; if tree-sitter node.children order is not source order, order may be wrong. | Check tree-sitter documentation for children order.

line 157-170 | low | Comment describes C/C++ declarator chain but the code for _declarator_name uses a loop that may not handle all cases; the bound of 16 is arbitrary. | Review if any real AST exceeds 16 links.
line 172-175 | low | parenthesized_declarator returns _ANON, which may miss valid function pointer names. | Verify if function pointer definitions should be named.

line 184-186 | low | reference_declarator falls back to unnamed children; comment says it carries inner declarator as unnamed child, but if the first named child is not the declarator, it might pick wrong node. | Test with a reference_declarator that has multiple named children.

line 198-201 | medium | Fallback scan for identifier/field_identifier/type_identifier may pick wrong name (e.g., return type) as noted in comment. | Ensure the fallback is only used when name and declarator fields are absent.

line 205-207 | uncheckable | _import_records function signature shown but body not in this chunk; cannot verify claim about being independent of internal_tops/known. | Review full function in later chunk.

claims.text: A recursive one blows Python's recursion limit on deeply nested real-world ASTs (long chained/generated expressions)
claims.why: The code implements an iterative pre-order walk using a stack, avoiding recursion.

claims.text: push children reversed so they pop back in source order.
claims.why: stack.extend(reversed(node.children)) ensures children are popped in original order.

claims.text: the name sits at the bottom of a declarator chain
claims.why: _declarator_name walks the chain via child_by_field_name('declarator') to find the name.

claims.text: the chain can be arbitrarily long, because pointer/reference/array returns each interpose a wrapper
the generic direct-children scan below used to return 'MyType' for 'MyType foo(void)'
claims.why: The fallback scan in _ts_name (line 198-201) does scan children for type_identifier, which could pick return type; the comment refers to previous behavior not in this chunk.

claims.text: a fabricated name is NOT filtered out of the clone passes
claims.why: Filtering logic for clone passes is not in this chunk.

claims.text: once a declarator field exists, its chain is authoritative and we never fall through to the scan.
claims.why: _ts_name checks for 'declarator' field before falling through to child scan.

claims.text: operator bool() is the one shape whose name node spans more than the name: the grammar's operator_cast covers the parameter list and cv qualifiers too, so slicing it whole yields 'operator bool() const'.
claims.why: _decl_text handles operator_cast by extracting text from start_byte to end of 'type' field, not full node.

claims.text: The depth bound is a guard against a malformed/adversarial tree, not an expected limit -- real declarator chains are two or three links.
claims.why: Loop in _declarator_name uses range(16) as bound.

claims.text: A function returning a function pointer -- 'int (*get_handler(int))(void)' -- nests a SECOND function_declarator inside parentheses, and which of the two is 'the function being defined' is genuinely ambiguous. Guessing here would fabricate a name, so under-report instead.
reference_declarator ('std::string& Cfg::name()') carries its inner declarator as an unnamed child rather than a labelled field.
claims.why: Code falls back to first named child when child_by_field_name('declarator') returns None.
